scope: Manchester, Salford, Liverpool and selectively researched surrounding towns; exact travel 9–14 November 2026 (5 nights, 4 full days), two experienced beer travellers. Cask/real ale, qualifying real cider/perry, distinctive pubs and worthwhile food. Extended excursions are alternatives.

venues.name: Angel
venues.why_visit: A worthwhile traditional-pub stop in Angel Meadow, where the modest old building sits among a rapidly changing skyline. The attraction is a rotating cask selection, a winter fire and the chance to turn a northern-centre beer walk into a proper pub meal. It fits naturally between the area’s stronger destination pubs without requiring a separate excursion. For experienced beer travellers, its value is the opportunity to investigate unfamiliar regional casks in an everyday freehouse setting; ask what has recently come on rather than expecting a fixed brewery showcase.
venues.beer: CAMRA describes six changing cask beers; the operator emphasises regional rotation. The house Fallen Angel bitter’s brewer is not disclosed in the cited listing.
venues.cider_note: CAMRA mentions two ciders but does not establish their current qualification as real cider. Ask for the producer and product before treating this as a cider destination.
venues.food: Seasonal pub dishes and sharing plates, with Sunday roasts. Check the current menu and reserve if the meal is central to your plan.
venues.visit_notes: CAMRA’s entry was updated in September 2026. The operator’s food and booking pages disagree about Wednesday kitchen service; confirm directly before relying on a Wednesday meal.
venues.transport: Combine on foot with Marble Arch, Smithfield Market Tavern and Crown & Kettle; Manchester Victoria and Shudehill are useful approaches.

venues.name: Balance Brewing & Blending
venues.why_visit: One of the most distinctive experiences for travellers who already know Europe’s beer cities. Balance concentrates on mixed-culture beer matured in barrels and also makes spontaneously fermented, barrel-aged cider from pressed apple juice. Visiting the taproom puts that process and its results together in one place, with bottles suitable for sharing. This earns a place through fermentation character and producer access rather than conventional cask breadth. It is an excellent focused addition to the Piccadilly cluster, especially if a cider-club event or tasting fits your exact dates.
venues.beer: Wild and sour beers are the core offering, with rotating draught and bottles. CAMRA says cask appears only very occasionally; do not plan on a regular cask range.
venues.cider_note: CAMRA explicitly flags real cider; the brewery documents its own spontaneously fermented, barrel-aged cider. Ask what is ready and available, plus guest cider/perry.
venues.food: CAMRA reports delivered pizza; confirm arrangements. The taproom does not establish a full kitchen.
venues.visit_notes: Normally Thursday–Sunday on the current official page. CAMRA reports ticketed Manchester Cider Club meetings, but no November session is assumed confirmed here.

The eccentric decor and informal format distinguish it from the more polished beer cafés. Its strongest role is as part of the Swan Street circuit: stop for a local or regional cask, inspect the continental list, and see whether a cider deserves attention. The combination gives the visit a different flavour from the nearby brewery-run Smithfield.

venues.cider_note: CAMRA explicitly reports real cider, without identifying a fixed current producer; ask at the bar.

venues.visit_notes: Walk-ins rather than table bookings. Beer and atmosphere are the reasons to visit; eat elsewhere for a full meal.

venues.why_visit: The strongest anchor for a Chorlton beer excursion. Formerly the Marble Beer House, it now combines Marble with independent guests in a compact, conversational setting. Its repeated local CAMRA recognition, including the documented 2026 branch award, adds a useful quality signal without replacing the practical reason to visit: a focused changing beer range in a neighbourhood pub. Pair it with Chorlton Tap and Fell for a coherent suburban circuit instead of scattering the day across unrelated outer-city venues.

Its best use is as a deliberate meal stop on a Salford circuit rather than a destination for maximum beer variety. The published British menus, Sunday service and advance-order sharing pies give you concrete options for making one pub visit a substantial food experience as well.

The preserved interior is the principal attraction, but current sources also establish an active cask offering after cellar work in 2026. Set aside time to explore the room layout with a drink and notice how the bar serves people sitting away from the front counter.

venues.venue_type: Working brewery and Indian vegetarian beer hall
venues.address: St James Building, 61–69 Oxford Street, Manchester, M1 6EQ
venues.why_visit: A particularly useful meal anchor for this trip, combining Indian vegetarian food with beer made in the same room. The tanks beneath the glass atrium make the production side visible while communal tables encourage a relaxed tasting-and-sharing meal. Its cask lines and CAMRA-listed real cider give it more relevance to your brief than a generic craft-beer restaurant. Choose this Manchester branch when the brewery experience matters: it adds a different setting to a day of old pubs and a substantial food break without abandoning the beer hunt.
venues.beer: The operator advertises two cask and sixteen keg lines, mixing Bundobust beers with collaborations and guests. Beer is produced on site; individual taps change.
venues.cider_note: CAMRA explicitly flags real cider and names Hogan’s. Check the current product and availability when ordering; the listing is not a live stock list.
venues.food: Indian vegetarian and vegan street-food dishes designed for sharing. The operator advertises its full food menu daily; reserve for a planned meal.
venues.visit_notes: Select the Oxford Street Brewery when booking: Manchester Piccadilly is a separate Bundobust. The official postcode is used here; CAMRA gives a different postcode for the same street address. Kitchen and bar closing times differ.
venues.transport: Near Manchester Oxford Road railway station and St Peter’s Square Metrolink; useful alongside the southern city-centre pubs.

venues.why_visit: A beer-focused café with enough cask depth to justify a stop even on a traditional-ale trip. Its bottle selection provides an opportunity to explore wild fermentation and sharing bottles without leaving the centre, and the cheese or meat plates offer a useful pause between pubs. It works particularly well with City Arms and the chop houses: the surroundings change completely, but beer remains the point. Make time to inspect the fridges and ask for a recommendation beyond whatever is easiest to recognise.

venues.food: Cheese and meat plates and other bar snacks are documented; useful for a light food stop.

Visit earlier if you want to examine the room quietly, or check the programme if an intimate gig would make the evening more interesting.

venues.name: Chorlton Tap

Its roots as The Bar make it part of the neighbourhood’s established beer culture rather than a recent generic taproom. The cider cool box is worth explicitly asking about; the selection can include perry as well as cider. Build it into a compact circuit with Beer House and Fell, and consider making it the food stop if the kitchen’s actual operating days fit your visit.

Combined with neighbouring Grey Horse, it offers an enjoyable comparison of two very small Manchester pubs. Avoid building a plan around arriving exactly at opening time: the current specialist listing explicitly cautions that hours can vary.

venues.name: Dee View Inn
venues.why_visit: A genuine community-pub alternative to modern micropubs, with intimate rooms, local character and a view towards the Dee Estuary. Its 2025 Wirral CAMRA Community Pub Award supports its inclusion, while the cask choice makes it more than a scenic detour. Combine with The Beer Lab if exploring cider in Heswall, but factor in the distance from the railway station.
venues.beer: Black Sheep Best Bitter and London Pride regularly listed, plus changing cask beers.
venues.cider_note: No qualifying real-cider selection established in the current listing.
venues.food: No kitchen; CAMRA explicitly allows customers to bring food or order takeaway.
venues.visit_notes: CAMRA lists opening from early afternoon daily. Tuesday is an advertised cask-club day, but verify the discount and event status.
venues.transport: Near Heswall centre; the railway station is significantly farther away than the nearby bus stops.

venues.name: Black Cat — Rose Lane
venues.address: 102 Rose Lane, Mossley Hill, Liverpool, L18 8AG
venues.why_visit: A purposeful south-Liverpool choice supported by inclusion on Liverpool CAMRA's 2026 Pub of the Year shortlist. The former Pi bar now offers rotating traditional and modern cask ales in an informal neighbourhood room. It is most useful when combining a Smithdown/Wavertree outing, rather than as part of the central Georgian-quarter walk. Specify Rose Lane: other Black Cat branches exist.
venues.beer: Three rotating cask beers covering modern and traditional styles according to CAMRA's July 2026 update.
venues.cider_note: No specifically evidenced qualifying real cider at this branch.
venues.food: No current substantial meal offer established.
venues.visit_notes: CAMRA lists daily afternoon/evening opening, earlier at weekends. No accessible toilet reported.
venues.transport: Near Mossley Hill railway station; also on local buses 61 and 80.

venues.name: Cobden Vaults
venues.why_visit: A worthwhile traditional local from Liverpool CAMRA's 2026 shortlisting, with convivial back-room conversation, changing regional cask and a character distinctly removed from the city-centre show pubs. The compact room and community atmosphere are the reasons to come. Woolton is a dedicated bus/taxi outing rather than a quick addition to a central pub crawl.
venues.beer: CAMRA lists three regular cask beers and one changing, including examples such as Landlord and White Rat; check the day’s board.
venues.cider_note: No current qualifying real cider established.
venues.food: No dependable meal offering established.
venues.visit_notes: CAMRA records daily service, with quizzes Monday/Tuesday and occasional weekend music. The detailed survey is older than the 2026 update; reconfirm.
venues.transport: Bus-based trip to Woolton village, not within walking distance of Liverpool Central or Lime Street.

venues.name: Fell Northern Quarter
venues.venue_type: Brewery-operated cask and cider beer bar
venues.why_visit: A strong addition when your city-centre afternoon is beer-led: Fell's Cumbrian ales, guests and a cider selection sit inside a converted listed building near Port Street and Piccadilly. It is especially useful on Tuesday, when several brewery taprooms are closed and CAMRA advertises a cask-club offer. Its beer focus gives it relevance beyond another modern keg bar, although it is not a historic pub interior.
venues.beer: Four changing cask lines alongside a larger keg selection; check whether any porter or mild is currently pouring. CAMRA says the changing cask is usually brewed by Fell, although an individual release is not a permanent fixture.
venues.cider_note: CAMRA marks real cider and describes boxed and bottled cider. Check specific producer and product; not every keg cider is automatically qualifying.
venues.food: Food provision unverified; use nearby pubs or food stalls.
venues.visit_notes: CAMRA lists Mon/Tue afternoon opening, with stairs at the main entrance and staff-assisted alternative access. Card only; check opening and cask-club terms.
venues.transport: Near Manchester Piccadilly and Piccadilly Gardens; useful alongside Port Street, Northern Monk and Café Beermoth.

sources.title: CAMRA: Fell Northern Quarter

venues.name: Pigeon Beer Wanderer
venues.venue_type: New railway-arch cask and craft beer bar
venues.why_visit: A June 2026 addition to the Piccadilly tasting cluster with an unusually broad advertised cask and keg choice for a new independent arch bar. It earns a specialist place for sheer beer-style breadth and an accessible stop near the station; food is available and the venue allows outside food. The attraction is discovery rather than traditional pub interiors, so keep it a flexible extra after the highest-priority Manchester pubs.
venues.beer: Four changing cask and about twenty keg lines documented by CAMRA; actual beers rotate.
venues.cider_note: No qualifying real-cider provision established in the current listing.
venues.food: Pizza is documented, and CAMRA says outside food is permitted; confirm the current arrangement.
venues.visit_notes: Closed Monday and Tuesday in the June/July 2026 entry. Wednesday first opens around 16:00, so it does not fit an early Stockport departure.
venues.transport: Under Manchester Piccadilly station at Sheffield Street; near Balance and Sureshot.

venues.name: Corner Post
venues.why_visit: A characterful small cask stop in a former post office, complete with the old postbox outside and displays of local history. This gives a Crosby/Waterloo excursion a second independent beer destination alongside The Coop. Cask variety and the real-cider badge are the reasons to choose it, while the room is especially suitable for a relaxed conversation.
venues.beer: Four changing cask ales from smaller breweries, with Colbier and Rock the Boat among the reported guest producers.
venues.cider_note: CAMRA marks real cider but does not establish the exact producer or product; confirm before committing to a cider-led detour.
venues.food: No full kitchen established; plan food elsewhere.
venues.visit_notes: CAMRA lists Monday closure and early evening closing; check before setting out from central Liverpool.
venues.transport: Within walking distance of Blundellsands & Crosby railway station; distinct from the central Liverpool pub district.
